name: Eye-area radiofrequency / Thermage eyes

lead: Eye-area radiofrequency, often called Thermage eyes after the Solta Medical device, aims to tighten loose eyelid skin and soften wrinkles around the eyes without surgery. People want a smoother, lifted, less hooded look.

RF energy heats the dermis, with a target around 67 C described, which prompts collagen and elastin remodeling so the skin firms over the following months. Sources describe the technique in general and list one registered trial of an electrosurgical device for wrinkles at the eye corners.

paras: It is done by a clinician in a short office session using a handheld device, often as a single treatment or a short series, with tightening developing gradually over weeks to months. People often combine it with other eye-area treatments and skincare.

Reported problems include pain severe enough to need sedation, skin dents from uneven healing, fat necrosis and atrophic scarring. The eye area is delicate and no eye-specific safety data were described in the sources reviewed. Choosing an experienced provider is the common precaution.

angle.text: Users seek radiofrequency treatments such as Thermage eyes to tighten loose eyelid skin and soften wrinkles without surgery. RF heats the deeper skin, collagen remodels and tightens, and the eye area looks smoother and more lifted. One registered trial of a device for eye-corner wrinkles exists.

lead: Eye-area radiofrequency treatment, often called Thermage eyes after the Thermage device brand, applies radiofrequency (RF) energy to the skin around the eyes to tighten loose skin, soften wrinkles and lift the brow slightly. It is marketed as a noninvasive alternative to surgery for people who want a firmer, less crepey eye area and a more open look without incisions or downtime [1].

RF skin tightening is described as heating the dermis to stimulate collagen, elastin and hyaluronic acid production [1]. Many manufacturers make such devices, including Solta Medical (Thermage), Venus Concept, Syneron, BTL and Lumenis [1].

A 2003 multicenter study of the original ThermaCool system, using single treatments around the eyes in 86 subjects, reported wrinkle score improvement in most blinded photo ratings and a measurable brow lift in many treated eyebrows [2].
infobox: At least 0.5 mm in 61.5% of eyebrows in a 2003 study [2]
2nd-degree burns 0.36% of applications in a 2003 study [2]

paras: RF devices use monopolar, bipolar or unipolar electrodes, which change how deep the energy penetrates [1]. Cited studies in the general literature include a blinded comparison of fractional RF with surgical facelift and studies showing new collagen and elastin formation, though several statements in the Wikipedia article carry citation-needed tags [1].
Wikipedia notes patients may report pain needing sedation, that improper application can leave dents from uneven healing, and that fat necrosis and atrophic scarring have been reported [1].

Radiofrequency skin tightening passes electrical energy through the skin to heat the dermis. Wikipedia describes the aim as stimulating production of collagen, elastin and hyaluronic acid, which reduces fine lines and loose skin, and says the dermal target temperature cited for remodeling and laxity reduction is 67 C, with treatment continuing until that temperature is reached [1]. Electrode configuration, whether monopolar, bipolar or unipolar, affects how deep the energy travels [1]. A 2011 study reported collagen and elastin changes in biopsies after a series of monopolar RF sessions [2]. Treatment around the eyes, where skin is thin, is the area the 2003 ThermaCool study targeted [2].

Wikipedia lists the Thermage line from Solta Medical among a large field of devices that includes Venus Freeze Plus and Venus Legacy (Venus Concept), VelaShape (Syneron), Exilis (BTL), V-Form (Viora), 3DEEP (Endymed) and tripolar devices from Lumenis and DEKA [1]. Microneedle RF products such as Profound (Candela), Fractora, Intensif and Genius (Lutronic) deliver energy through needles that penetrate the skin, and microneedle RF has FDA approval for cellulite reduction [1].

Heat can also be used for fat reduction when skin cooling is adjusted, and RF is used on the jowls, abdomen, thighs and arms as well as the face [1]. Alternatives that Wikipedia mentions include laser resurfacing and some ultrasound-based treatments [1].

The 2003 multicenter study described a single session around the eyes with follow-up at 6 months, with edema and erythema rarely reported [2]. Wikipedia reports that some patients experienced pain severe enough to require sedation [1]. Results are described as appearing over months as collagen remodels, which is the pattern the 2003 study captured over 6 months [2].

Within looksmaxxing and appearance forums, eye-area RF is discussed as one of the non-surgical options for the periorbital region, alongside fillers, lasers and blepharoplasty, for people seeking a firmer, more open eye area. T Nation posters discussing loose skin after weight loss have asked about energy-based options when surgeons decline to operate [3]. No community protocol exists, since treatment is performed by clinicians with professional devices.

Reported adverse effects include second-degree burns (0.36 percent of applications in the 2003 study, with three patients having small residual scars at 6 months) [2], skin dents from improper application with uneven healing, fat necrosis and atrophic scarring [1]. Wikipedia reports that applying vacuum at the treatment point reduced burning and crusting, a statement tagged as needing citation [1].

A 2003 multicenter study in Lasers in Surgery and Medicine treated 86 subjects once with the ThermaCool TC system and followed them for 6 months. Blinded photograph scoring showed a Fitzpatrick wrinkle score improvement of at least 1 point in 83.2 percent of treated periorbital areas, while treating physicians, without pre-treatment photographs, noted improvement in 28.9 percent. Half of subjects were satisfied or very satisfied with wrinkle reduction, and 61.5 percent of eyebrows were lifted by at least 0.5 mm. Edema and erythema were rare, second-degree burns occurred in 0.36 percent of applications (21 of 5,858), and three patients had small residual scars at 6 months [2].

A 2011 study in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology treated six people with six sessions of monopolar RF at two-week intervals and measured histology: it reported noticeable clinical improvement with high satisfaction and objective changes in elastin and collagen in biopsies [2].

A registered single-blind, paired-design, non-inferiority device trial (n=80, completed, started 2024) assessed a universal electrosurgical device for temporary improvement of mild and moderate wrinkles around the eye corners and cheek folds [4]. No results were available for this entry.

timeline.event: Multicenter study reports periorbital tightening with ThermaCool RF [2]
Study documents collagen and elastin changes after RF sessions [2]
Registered trial of an electrosurgical device for eye-corner wrinkles begins [4]
